caseStudies.title: Browser Focus Mode Extension
caseStudies.cardSummary: Designed a browser productivity extension for deep work: blocking distractions, enforcing session timers, and applying Calm Technology principles to reduce interruption without friction.
caseStudies.summary: A Chrome extension that flips the focus blocker model: instead of blocking what distracts you, it defines what you need. Full product arc from discovery interviews through PRD, metrics, roadmap, and Calm Technology principles.

content.text: When a user is trying to focus in a particular browser tab, the presence of other open tabs, along with the ability to open new ones, creates a constant source of distraction. The average user has 17 tabs open at any given time, and productivity communities consistently identify tab-switching as a primary focus killer.
Discovery method: Personal experience as a proxy user, validated through five structured user interviews. Core discipline: ask about the past, never the future.
Sample interview questions:

items: "Tell me about an instance where you felt distracted by multiple tabs open in your browser."
"Tell me about the last time you had to do focused work. What was the setup you had in place before starting?"
"Walk me through a time when, despite all measures you had in place, you still ended up getting distracted."

content.text: Primary segment: Students and knowledge workers doing self-directed deep work without a hard external deadline enforcing focus.

Jobs To Be Done: When a student or knowledge worker is trying to focus on a task and is feeling distracted, they want to accomplish the task at hand successfully within a given time, so they can finish what they set out to do and feel their time was genuinely well spent.
Key insight: The real job is not "block distracting websites." It is "create conditions where I can do my best work and feel the satisfaction of finishing what I started."

rows: Cold Turkey
Block what distracts you
Most aggressive blocker; application-level whitelisting
No browser-level tab control; cannot define an intentional workspace
Freedom
Cross-platform restriction with scheduling
Available on mobile; syncs across devices
Same subtractive model; no tab-level workspace control
StayFocusd
Lightweight browser-based time limits
Free Chrome extension; simple to set up
Time limits cap distraction but don't prevent it; no workspace concept

content.text: Cold Turkey blocks what you don't want. This extension defines what you do want. That is the difference between building walls and building a room.

A Chrome extension allowing users to initiate a timed focus session capped at 90 minutes. Once a session begins, the browser enters a locked state: the user cannot switch to any tab outside a pre-defined group of approved tabs. If a user attempts to exit before the timer completes, they see a 15-second countdown to confirm. The goal is pause, not punishment.
Non-goals for v1: No customisable UI · No session lockout · No Pomodoro timer · No cross-device sync · Chrome only

rows: North Star
Distinct users completing 2+ focus sessions per week
Signals habit formation, not just trial
Guardrail
Uninstall rate after sessions
Catches long-term failure even when short-term looks healthy
Input (30 days)
Users completing 15+ sessions in first month
Signal the product has become routine, not novelty
Tab locking with interval sessions (max 90 min)
Tab border highlighting (Calm Tech Principle 5)
Motivational quotes on exit, only after user testing
Chained tab groups (approved workspace)
Countdown before session starts (Calm Tech Principle 2)
Session completion celebration
15-second countdown exit mechanism
Peripheral time indicator (Calm Tech Principle 3)
Optional to-do list, only if validated

items: Exit friction over hard lockout: 15-second countdown trades absolute enforcement for user trust.
Chrome only in v1: Covers ~65% of browser market share. A polished Chrome experience beats a mediocre multi-browser one.
No customisation in v1: Personalising a focus app contradicts its core purpose (Calm Technology Principle 1).

caseStudies.title: Spotify: Discover Music
caseStudies.cardSummary: A strategic recommendation to solve genuine music discovery for the niche listener segment using a two-layer data architecture: behavioral history plus a community music intelligence layer trained on genre-specific listener communities.
caseStudies.summary: A strategic recommendation to solve genuine music discovery for the niche listener segment. Spotify's existing infrastructure creates a structural ceiling: the more specific a user's taste, the less useful features become over time. Discover Music proposes a natural language discovery mode powered by a two-layer data architecture including a community music intelligence layer.

content.text: Spotify's recommendation engine is not broken. It is working exactly as designed. The algorithm is a feedback loop that prioritizes songs with more global consumption data, structurally favoring popular content and marginalizing niche artists. The algorithm shifted further toward familiarity in 2025 — Autoplay, the AI DJ, and Song Radio now recycle tracks users already know.

Only 27% of users agree that streaming services help them discover music outside familiar territory. 42% actively disagree. That gap represents hundreds of millions of users whose primary discovery need is unmet by everything Spotify currently offers, many of them premium subscribers.

Spotify attempted niche discovery through Discovery Mode, but that works for mid-tier artists trying to break through — not for artists whose ceiling is genuinely small. The structural problem is data architecture. Every existing feature begins from listening history and finds something adjacent. Discover Music removes that ceiling entirely.
Primary persona: 25 to 35-year-old with eclectic cross-genre taste. Listens seriously. Pays for premium.

rows: Current behavior
Uses Smart Shuffle and Discover Weekly. After a few days, recommendations become cyclic. Retreats to familiar songs when discovery stops working.
Discovery loop
When Spotify fails them, they find music outside the app through social media, friend recommendations, or YouTube. The app is where they store music after discovery has happened elsewhere.
Core frustration
Installed a music app to expand their musical world. Using it as a jukebox for songs they already know.
Switching cost
Years of behavioral history trained Spotify's algorithm to their specific taste. That history does not transfer to any competing platform — arriving at YouTube Music means starting cold.

content.text: The Two Jobs:

items: Job 1 (Spotify does well): Serve me well within what I already know and love. High switching cost keeps users embedded despite discovery frustrations.
Job 2 (Spotify fails structurally): Take me somewhere I have never been but know I would love. This job cannot be completed with behavioral data alone — it requires a different data source.

content.text: Spotify knows what a user has heard. It cannot know what a user has not yet heard but would love. That gap cannot be closed by a better algorithm trained on the same data.

rows: Spotify
761M MAUs, unmatched behavioral data depth, strongest algorithmic discovery infrastructure, 100M+ track catalog.
Recommendation engine anchored to listening history. Structurally biased toward popular content. Niche listeners hit a cyclic recommendation ceiling regardless of time on platform.
Apple Music
Spatial Audio and lossless quality at no extra cost. Over 100 human editors globally curating genre-specific playlists — the deepest editorial curation in the market.
Apple-only, excluding all Android users. Editorial curation is passive: the user cannot tell Apple Music what they are looking for. No intent-based discovery mechanism exists.
YouTube Music
Broader content including live sessions, covers, and unofficial recordings. Leverages over a decade of YouTube watch history as behavioral signal.
Switching means losing years of algorithm training no migration tool can transfer. Discovery designed for clear genre preferences, not cross-genre listeners.

content.text: Every existing discovery feature begins from what a user already listens to or relies on passive editorial decisions. None have built a mechanism where the user states their intent and the product steps entirely outside their history to fulfill it. That is the gap Discover Music fills.

A new tile on the Spotify home screen called Discover Music. When tapped, users enter a dedicated discovery session where they describe the kind of music they want in their own words. Spotify generates a playlist drawing from the full catalogue — not just listening history — and presents it with a visual map showing how familiar or unfamiliar each track is.
Three differentiators from the AI DJ:

items: Text input over conversational persona: The DJ accepts voice commands through a persona. Discover Music accepts written descriptions, anchoring output to specific user intent rather than a DJ's interpretation.
Full track playback: The DJ plays partial tracks for background listening. Discover Music plays every track completely, serving the job of finding music to save and return to.

Intensity filter with a history-off mode: Take it easy (70% familiar, 30% new), Go crazy (30% familiar, 70% new), and Music from another planet (listening history ignored entirely). The DJ cannot offer a history-off mode by design.

content.text: The Community Intelligence Layer: Current Spotify infrastructure matches descriptions against acoustic similarity and catalogue metadata. Discover Music adds a community intelligence layer built from genre-specific listener discussion communities seeded and moderated by Spotify directly. NLP extracts connections between artists, sounds, moods, and eras that no acoustic algorithm can replicate.

10 launch communities seeded 2–3 months before release: Hip-Hop, Pop, Rock, Electronic/EDM, Latin, R&B/Soul, K-Pop, Afrobeats, Country, and Indie/Alternative. Minimum 500 posts per genre community before launch. Below this threshold the feature defaults to catalogue metadata.

Discovery is already Spotify's strongest retention lever. AI-powered features drive 40% higher retention rates and 140 minutes of daily listening versus 99 minutes for non-AI users. Personalized playlists contribute to 46% of premium conversions.

The 42% of users who feel discovery features are not serving them are being structurally excluded by an architecture that cannot serve them without a different data source. They are not generating return on Spotify's existing discovery investment.

At 293 million premium subscribers paying approximately $11 per month, a 1% improvement in premium retention represents over $38 million in annualised revenue. Discover Music targets users showing playlist fatigue signals — the cohort at highest churn risk — making it a direct revenue protection play.

rows: Phase 1 (0–30 days)
Playlist fatigue users — premium subscribers who have not added new music in 30+ days
Quality validation in hardest conditions. If it re-engages this cohort, the retention story is direct and commercially significant.
Phase 2 (30–90 days)
Power users — premium subscribers with high Discover Weekly engagement
Retention reinforcement. A/B test the Discovery Map visual. Monitor correlation with artist follows and playlist saves.
Phase 3 (90+ days)
All premium users, then free tier 6 months later
Full platform scale. Free tier: 3 sessions/week, ad-supported, hard wall upgrade prompt at limit.
Major label conflict over stream diversion to independent artists
High without proactive management
Negotiate minimum stream percentage guarantee for major label content before launch. Surface through deep catalog tracks, not exclusively independent artists.
Playlist quality misses: generated playlist feels irrelevant to description
High in early iterations
Closed beta with tight feedback loop. In-session prompt: "Did you discover something you would not have found otherwise?" Use responses to calibrate before broad release.
Community intelligence layer low signal in niche genres
Medium
Seed 10 genre communities 2–3 months before launch with minimum 500 posts each. Layer 1 catalogue data acts as fallback when community signal is thin.
Feature cannibalises AI DJ without adding net new engagement
Low
Monitor DJ cannibalisation rate. Full track playback and history-off mode serve a fundamentally different use case than the DJ.

content.text: Primary: Feature-attributed track saves — songs first encountered through Discover Music subsequently saved to liked songs or a personal playlist, measured against a baseline of saves from standard recommendations.
Downstream:

items: Post-discovery artist follows: users who follow a new artist after a Discover Music session
Session return rate: users who complete more than one session within 30 days
Playlist fatigue conversion rate: percentage of fatigue-cohort users who return to active music-adding behavior within 30 days of first session
Free-to-premium conversion rate: percentage of free users who upgrade after hitting the three-session weekly limit

content.text: Guardrails:

items: Session abandonment rate within the first 60 seconds
Label stream distribution: percentage of Discover Music-generated streams going to major label content, tracked against the negotiated minimum guarantee
